egg.diagnostics: Reddish-orange, pea-sized eggs buried in a gravel nest (redd) in headwater riffle habitat; not normally seen during field surveys.
egg.notes: Incubation 6-12 weeks depending on water temperature; hatches to an alevin still attached to a yolk sac (~2 cm).

fry.diagnostics: Post-yolk-sac fry feeding on stream invertebrates, before parr marks fully develop.

parr.diagnostics: 8-11 oval parr marks along the lateral line, each about the width of the eye or narrower, often with a single red/orange spot between adjacent marks. Adipose fin plain grey/dusky with no orange or red pigment. Maxilla (upper jaw) short, not reaching past the rear margin of the eye. Only 1-4 spots on the gill cover, often just one large spot. Pectoral fin relatively long and pointed; caudal fin deeply forked.
parr.notes: Parr reside in freshwater 2-6 years in Nova Scotia's often-acidic Southern Upland streams before smolting.

juvenile.diagnostics: Smolt stage: parr marks fade under a silvery guanine layer; back darkens to steel-blue/olive, flanks bright silver.

adult.diagnostics: Fusiform, laterally compressed, silvery fresh from the sea, becoming bronze/brown with scattered black spots (often X- or cross-shaped, concentrated above the lateral line) after time in freshwater. Mouth terminal, maxilla reaching only to about the rear margin of the eye, not past it. Adipose fin plain, without red/orange margin or spots. Caudal fin moderately to deeply forked, more square-edged in large multi-sea-winter fish. Spawning males develop a hooked lower jaw (kype).
adult.sizeRange: Grilse (1 sea-winter): <63 cm fork length, 1-3 kg. Multi-sea-winter adults: ~63-105 cm, 3-7+ kg.

lookalikeSpecies.distinguishingNote: Brown trout maxilla extends well past the rear of the eye (salmon's does not); brown trout has larger, more numerous dark spots with pale halos, often extending onto an adipose fin with a red/orange margin (salmon's adipose fin is plain); brown trout's tail is nearly square in adults vs. salmon's deeply forked tail.
Brook trout show pale wavy vermiculations on the back and dorsal/caudal fins (absent in salmon) and white-leading-edge lower fins backed by a black stripe; salmon lack both.
Rainbow trout have small black spots densely covering the caudal fin in rows and, in maturing fish, a pink lateral band; salmon show few or no tail spots and no pink stripe.

species.habitatNotes: Cold, well-oxygenated headwater rivers and tributaries with gravel/cobble spawning and rearing substrate. Major NS rivers include the Margaree, St. Marys, LaHave, and Medway, plus Eastern Shore and Southern Upland systems; DFO's Gulf Nova Scotia program monitors index rivers including the Margaree, West River Antigonish, East River Pictou, and River Philip. Inner Bay of Fundy river populations are listed Endangered by COSEWIC. Adults spend part of their life at sea, returning to natal rivers to spawn.

species.habitatNotes: Anadromous; in Atlantic Canada only two confirmed spawning populations remain: the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence (Miramichi River) and the Bay of Fundy system, whose only currently robust spawning run is Nova Scotia's Shubenacadie-Stewiacke river system. That population overwinters in Grand Lake and Shubenacadie Lake and migrates through the hypertidal Minas Passage of the Bay of Fundy. Other Bay of Fundy-area stocks (Annapolis River NS; Saint John River NB) are severely depressed or possibly extirpated. The Bay of Fundy population was designated Endangered by COSEWIC in 2012; invasive chain pickerel in Shubenacadie overwintering habitat is flagged as an emerging threat.

juvenile.diagnostics: Resembles small adults; silvery, deep-bodied, with a sawtooth (serrated/keeled) belly scale row along the midline. adult.diagnostics: Key pair-ID vs. blueback herring: alewife has a white (pale) peritoneum (body cavity lining) vs. blueback's black/dusky peritoneum — the single most reliable distinguishing character. Alewife also has a larger eye diameter (greater than snout length) vs. blueback's smaller eye (≤ snout length), and generally a greater body depth. Alewife back is more blue-grey/greenish (less deep blue) than blueback. Both species: deep-bodied, laterally compressed, silvery with a single dark shoulder spot behind the operculum, sawbelly keel of scales between pelvic and anal fins, single soft dorsal fin, deeply forked caudal fin.
adult.sizeRange: Adults typically 25-30 cm total length; spawning adults average ~279-305 mm.

lookalikeSpecies.distinguishingNote: Classic tough field pair. Best character: peritoneum colour (alewife white/pale, blueback black/sooty). In NS rivers, alewife typically arrive first in spring runs, blueback herring follow about 2 weeks later.

Alewife/blueback lack an adipose fin (present in smelt) and lack strong canine teeth on the tongue/jaws that smelt have; juvenile Atlantic herring (a marine visitor) lacks the sawbelly keel of scutes that alewife/blueback have.

species.habitatNotes: Anadromous; NS populations run into rivers/lakes each spring (May-June) to spawn, historically the target of the Gaspereau River commercial fishery (weir/dip-net gear), one of the largest gaspereau fisheries in the Maritimes, with associated fishway/fish-lift infrastructure on the Gaspereau River. Over 69 rivers along Atlantic coastal Nova Scotia and additional Bay of Fundy/Gulf of St. Lawrence systems support spawning gaspereau runs (alewife + blueback herring collectively). DFO manages the fishery under the Gaspereau Integrated Fishery Management Plan.

lookalikeSpecies.distinguishingNote: Pumpkinseed's continuous single dorsal fin, small round body, and orange-red-bordered opercular spot separate it from yellow perch (two well-separated dorsal fins, elongate barred body) and smallmouth bass (larger, more elongate, only a shallow dorsal-fin notch, no opercular ear spot).

species.habitatNotes: Reported as present in Nova Scotia lakes in DFO and general angling sources, but its native-vs-introduced status specifically in this province is unresolved from sources checked in this research pass: some range descriptions place the native Atlantic Slope limit at New Brunswick (at or just south of NS), and it is not listed among the species NS's Invasive Species Council currently flags as a priority invasive fish concern (unlike chain pickerel and smallmouth bass). Treat the native-status field as unverified pending direct ACCDC/DFO confirmation; likely a common catch in vegetated NS lake margins regardless of origin.

citations.accessedNote: Confirms pumpkinseed presence in Nova Scotia waters; general identification and biology.
